slides.say: At a sports camp, swimmers make up five twelfths of all the campers, and the rest are runners. Which could be the difference between the numbers of runners and swimmers?

They don't tell us how many campers there are, only a fraction. So we can't find the difference exactly. They ask what it could be. So we'll find a rule that the difference must follow, and rule out the choices that break it.
Let's start with the math way, with ratio units. Remember, a fraction of the whole is a ratio. Swimmers are five out of twelve, so the swimmers are five x, and all the campers are twelve x.
at: a fraction of the whole is a ratio
so the swimmers are five x

slides.say: The rest are runners. Twelve x minus five x is seven x.
The difference between the runners and the swimmers is seven x minus five x, two x.
at: seven x minus five x, two x

slides.say: What does two x tell us? x is the size of one unit, a number of campers, so x is a whole number. Two times a whole number is always even. So the difference must be even.
Now the choices. Twenty-one is odd, so choice number one is out. Fifteen is odd, so choice number three is out. Nineteen is odd, so choice number four is out.
at: so choice number one is out
so choice number three is out
so choice number four is out

slides.say: Only twenty-two is even. And they ask what could be, so one case that really works is enough. Two x is twenty-two, so x is eleven. Five times eleven is fifty-five swimmers. And seven times eleven is seventy-seven runners.
Seventy-seven minus fifty-five is twenty-two. It works. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: This works for every part of a ratio. The swimmers are five x, so their number divides by five. The runners divide by seven. And all the campers, twelve x, divide by twelve. So when a ratio counts people, the total always divides by the sum of the ratio numbers. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
